claims.text: The starting material is a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating produced under standard deposition conditions.
The starting coating has a baseline population of nano-precipitates located at FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Changing cooling rate or spraying distance can increase and tailor nano-precipitate density and distribution at FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
At moderately elevated temperature, thermally activated creep mechanisms dominate the coating's deformation.
The proposed loading conditions can activate creep without causing excessive precipitate coarsening.
The intervention produces a higher density of well-distributed nano-precipitates along FCC/BCC boundaries.
A denser nano-precipitate dispersion at interphase boundaries pins dislocations more effectively.
Precipitate pinning increases the stress required for dislocation movement by climb or bypass.
Increasing interphase-boundary nano-precipitate density reduces the creep strain rate under sustained loading.
Increasing interphase-boundary nano-precipitate density delays the onset of tertiary creep.
Baseline coatings exhibit progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
The proposed mechanism operates only below the temperature at which precipitates become unstable or coarsen excessively.
The proposed mechanism operates while applied stress remains within the coating's structural-integrity limits.
Other microstructural factors and deposition variability may affect the magnitude and optimum density of the precipitate-mediated creep response.
